summary:
Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults in private has been legal in Montserrat since 2001. The reform was effected retrospectively by an Order in Council under Sections 3(1) and 3(7) of the Caribbean Territories (Criminal Law) Order, 2000. It formed part of a single British decision to scrap anti-gay statutes in five Caribbean territories, including Montserrat and Turks & Caicos, on the stated ground that the laws violated signed international human rights agreements. The order reached Montserrat from London over the objections of local politicians and religious leaders rather than with their consent.

Residual criminal exposure remains and is defined by the sex of the partners. Lesbian activity was never an offence in Montserrat. Group sex and sex in public remain criminal offences for everyone. The age of consent is set at 18 for homosexual activity against 16 for heterosexual activity, so conduct that would be lawful between opposite-sex partners of the same age can be an offence between same-sex partners.

Montserrat's constitutional and statutory framework prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation. Article 16 of the Montserrat Constitution and Article 79 of the Labour Code ban such discrimination, with 'discriminatory' defined as affording different treatment on grounds such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion or other status. As a British Overseas Territory, Montserrat must also comply with international human rights instruments, including the European Convention on Human Rights and its non-discrimination and equality obligations.

Relationship recognition does not extend to same-sex couples. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal. Article 10(1) of the Constitution protects only opposite-sex marriage, stating that every man and woman of marriageable age has the right to marry a person of the opposite sex and to found a family.

A visitor should expect almost no visible organised LGBT social infrastructure. Montserrat has no gay bars, nightclubs or other dedicated venues. Several hotels on the island welcome gay tourists and operate non-discrimination policies, which is the main documented point of entry for a visitor seeking a welcoming environment.
tangentialFactors:
The scarcity of visible LGBT life on Montserrat has physical as well as social causes. Reporting from GlobalGayz in September 2012 describes a 104 km2 island reshaped by Hurricane Hugo in 1989 and the 1995 Soufriere Hills eruption, which wastelanded the south and displaced more than half the population northward. The same account characterises the local social scene as decimated, capturing the mood with the observation that gay people 'are everywhere but hardly here'.

The 2001 decriminalisation was a regional package rather than a Montserrat-specific negotiation: Britain removed anti-gay statutes in five Caribbean territories at once, naming Montserrat and Turks & Caicos among them, and framed the change as compliance with international human rights agreements. The Associated Press reported the accompanying cultural rift with London, with local politicians and religious leaders opposed to a reform delivered from outside.
localsOnly:
Residents hold a constitutional and statutory right not to be discriminated against on grounds including sexual orientation, with Article 16 of the Montserrat Constitution and Article 79 of the Labour Code providing the operative bans and the definition of 'discriminatory' covering sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion or other status. The Labour Code provision is the resident-facing route for employment complaints.

The same residents live under an age-of-consent differential of 18 for homosexual activity against 16 for heterosexual activity, and under a marriage provision, Article 10(1) of the Constitution, that guarantees the right to marry only a person of the opposite sex. Group sex and sex in public remain offences regardless of the partners' sex.

Local politicians and religious leaders opposed the 2001 decriminalisation, and the reform was imposed by an order from London rather than enacted with local consent, which remains the political context in which the non-discrimination provisions sit.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory addresses legal gender recognition, change of gender markers on passports or identity documents, non-binary recognition, access to gender-affirming healthcare, or hate-crime provisions covering gender identity. Whether Montserrat's constitutional and Labour Code non-discrimination language is applied to gender identity, as distinct from sexual orientation, is not sourced here and should be treated as unresolved.

The inventory does not document enforcement of Article 16 or Article 79, any complaints brought under them, or any recorded incident of violence against a trans or gender-nonconforming visitor. The description of Montserrat's social scene derives from a single 2012 report and may not reflect the present position; the same applies to the claim that several hotels operate non-discrimination policies, whose terms for trans guests are not specified in the sources.
